title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: tools/story story/ top-level files
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: tools/story story/ top-level files. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.7 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.7 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.7 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.7) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under tools/story story/ top-level files. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/story story/ top-level files. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/story story/ top-level files to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/story story/ top-level files; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/story story/ top-level files plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/story story/ top-level files that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/ssr-node. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/ssr-node to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/ssr-node; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/ssr-node plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/ssr-node that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: A released resource entry is collected 0 to :gc-after-ms after its last owner leaves; measure GC from the final release
description:
A released resource entry is garbage-collected anywhere from 0 to `:gc-after-ms` after its last owner leaves, rather than after a full warm window.

## Today

GC arms when the entry settles. It re-arms only when its check finds an owner still attached. Releasing the last owner cancels polls but leaves the GC timer alone. `release-owner-from-identities` in `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/events.cljc` (~L2044) says: "the stale / GC timers stay armed — an owner-free entry still GCs". Spec 016 (~L1236) codifies this: "a later owner release does not restart an armed timer".

So an entry released 4m59s into a 5-minute cycle is collected one second later. Yet 016 (~L307) justifies the warm window as letting "a quick re-attach (a route bounce, a remount) reuse the cached data", and the timing defeats exactly that. The docs were aligned to the code (rf2-rzsv5, rf2-n2onr, rf2-m9uqu) without any ruling that the current timing is wanted.

## Change

When an entry becomes owner-free, re-arm GC with the partial re-arm the GC-skip path already emits: `[:rf.resource/schedule-timers {… :timers {:gc gc-delay}}]` in `events.cljc` (~L3614).

Preserve:
- the settle-time arm, so that ownerless prefetch is still collected;
- `:gc-after-ms :never`, which still arms nothing.

Do NOT add a new timer kind or a knob.

## Text to update

- Spec 016: ~L303, ~L1236, ~L1247.
- The gc-kind and `cancel-for-key!` docstrings in `timers.cljc`.
- `docs/api/re-frame.resources.md` (~L118).
- `docs/resources/coming-from-tanstack-query.md`: ~L20 and its GC row. Final-release GC is also what TanStack Query users expect.

No hot-zone file.

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\opus-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\resources.md` §11, and `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\15-resources.md` §2. title: Unit-test pruning: ssr-ring
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/ssr-ring/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/ssr-ring/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/ssr-ring/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/ssr-ring/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/ssr-ring/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/ssr-ring/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/ssr-ring/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: re-frame.core-schemas defines three read wrappers nothing calls, served by two late-bind hooks nothing else reads; delete them
description:
`re-frame.core-schemas` defines three read wrappers that nothing calls, and they are served by two late-bind hooks that nothing else reads. Delete them.

## Where

`implementation/core/src/re_frame/core_schemas.cljc` defines five `defwrapper`s. `re-frame.core` re-exports only `reg-app-schema` and `reg-app-schemas`, and its own comment (~L1131) says the schema reads are "not re-exported from `re-frame.core`" and live on `re-frame.schemas`.

The three read wrappers are `app-schema-meta`, `app-schemas` and `app-schemas-digest`:
- they have no callers: `git grep -F 'core-schemas/app'` over tracked Clojure files is empty;
- Xray calls `rf.schemas/app-schema-meta` directly;
- their docstrings promise nil or `{}` "when the schemas artefact is not on the classpath", a path no code reaches.

Two hooks exist only to serve them: `:schemas/app-schema-meta` and `:schemas/app-schemas`. They are published in `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas.cljc` (~L123-124, `(rf.late-bind/set-fn! :schemas/app-schema-meta app-schema-meta)`), with directory rows in `late_bind/directory.cljc` (~L315-320).

## Change

Delete:
- the three wrappers;
- those two hook publications and their two directory rows.

`core-schemas` then wraps only the two registrars, which is the shape Conventions §Optional-artefact wrapper convention gives SSR.

Keep:
- `:schemas/app-schemas-digest`, which epoch (`assembly.cljc`), SSR (`hydrate.cljc`) and Story (`identity.cljc`) read;
- every `re-frame.schemas` var.

Also correct `tools/xray/spec/021-Dynamic-Panel-Designs.md` (~L3452), which says Xray goes through "the `:schemas/app-schema-meta` late-bind hook".

No hot-zone file.

title: A queued GC check collects a recreated entry when remove/populate reuses its window number
description:
Merged-PR audit #11317, merge 4c8db1ddc6c0518eaffdaa2c18cd6ef0471dbc3d. GC windows are counters stored on each cache entry. Removing an entry discards its counter, so a mutation that populates the same key starts again at window 1. An already queued check from the removed entry's window 1 is then accepted by gc-fired-handler and immediately collects the new entry.

Confirmed with the PR's virtual host clock, held router drains, real timer thunk and real mutation reply. title: Unit-test pruning: derivation-conformance
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/derivation-conformance/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/derivation-conformance/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/derivation-conformance/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/derivation-conformance/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/derivation-conformance/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/derivation-conformance/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/derivation-conformance/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: After a hot-reloaded app-db schema change, every later event is rejected, even events that never touch the changed path
description:
## Bug

In a dev build, hot-reloading an app-db schema so that the live value at its path no longer conforms makes every later `:db`-writing event fail, including events that never touch that path. Each one is rejected, and the error names the innocent event as `:failing-id`. The app looks frozen until something rewrites the stale slice, which contradicts Spec 010's promise that "the live app continues running".

## Evidence

**Where (trunk 475bdcaacf):**
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc:1289-1290`: the router hands `:schemas/validate-app-schema!` only the candidate `db-after`.
- `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc:919-937`: `validate-app-schema!` loops over every entry of `frame-schema-entries` and validates `(get-in db registered-path)` for each, whatever the event changed. Any failure fails the whole candidate.
- `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/storage.cljc:650-656`: re-registration swaps the new schema in first, then `maybe-emit-schema-violation!` (`:512-575`) emits a `:warning :rf.schema/violation` with `:recovery :logged-and-skipped`. From then on, every commit re-validates the stale slice against the new schema.

**Repro (*probed*, `clojure -M` from `implementation/schemas`, plain-atom substrate, at 989a1c6d53, which is identical to 475bdcaacf for `implementation/core/src` and `implementation/schemas`; first run at 9e84689562 gave the same result):**

```clojure
(rf/init! plain-atom/adapter)
(rf/reg-event :u/seed (fn [{:keys [db]} _] {:db (assoc db :user {:name "a"})}))
(rf/reg-event :u/fix  (fn [{:keys [db]} _] {:db (assoc db :user {:name "a" :email "a@b"})}))
(rf/reg-event :n/inc  (fn [{:keys [db]} _] {:db (update db :n (fnil inc 0))}))
(rf/make-frame {:id :probe/f})
(rf/with-frame :probe/f (rf/reg-app-schema [:user] [:maybe [:map [:name :string]]]))
(rf/dispatch-sync [:u/seed] {:frame :probe/f})
(rf/dispatch-sync [:n/inc]  {:frame :probe/f})        ;=> {:user {:name "a"}, :n 1}
;; "hot reload": [:user] now requires :email
(rf/with-frame :probe/f
  (rf/reg-app-schema [:user] [:maybe [:map [:name :string] [:email :string]]]))
;; trace: [:warning :rf.schema/violation {:path [:user]}]
(rf/dispatch-sync [:n/inc] {:frame :probe/f})
(rf/dispatch-sync [:n/inc] {:frame :probe/f})         ;=> {:user {:name "a"}, :n 1}   both refused
;; trace, per :n/inc: [:error :rf.error/schema-validation-failure
;;   {:path [:user :email], :failing-id :n/inc, :where :app-db, ...}]
(rf/dispatch-sync [:u/fix] {:frame :probe/f})
(rf/dispatch-sync [:n/inc] {:frame :probe/f})         ;=> {..., :n 2}   unfreezes only after [:user] is rewritten
```

**Contract:** Spec 010 §Schema migration on hot-reload (line 823): the runtime emits `:rf.schema/violation` "so dev panels highlight the stale slice; the live app continues running", with recovery `:logged-and-skipped`. In practice the slice is not skipped. It blocks every commit, and §Per-step recovery row 4 (line 183) then blames whichever event happens to commit next.

## Expected

After a schema hot-reload, events that do not change the stale slice commit normally. An event that writes an invalid value at a registered path is still rejected and named.

## Fix direction

Minimal, with no new modes:
- Pass `db-before` to `:schemas/validate-app-schema!`.
- Skip a registered path when its slice is present in both dbs and `identical?` between `db-before` and `db-after`. A parent path is still checked when a child under it changed, and `[]` is checked whenever the db changed, because those slices are not identical.
- Leave absent slices checked as today. That keeps current boot-window behaviour (non-nullable unseeded siblings, the `[:maybe …]` idiom) out of this fix.
- Whether a never-written slice should block commits at all is a separate question for Mike (Opus open question 5), and this bead does not need it answered.
- Optional, and only if wanted: extend `maybe-emit-schema-violation!` to a FIRST registration over a present, non-conforming slice. That means dropping its `prior-registered?` gate and amending 010's "the first registration of a path emits nothing". It is not required to fix the freeze.

Update 010 §Schema migration on hot-reload and §When schemas are checked to state the resulting guarantee: every installed value at a registered path conforms, or a `:rf.schema/violation` named it when its schema changed.

## Acceptance

- New JVM test in `implementation/schemas/test/`, using the probe above. After re-registering `[:user]` to require `:email`, `:n/inc` installs, and exactly one `:rf.schema/violation` names `[:user]`. It fails at trunk.
- An event writing an invalid `[:user]` is still rejected, with itself as `:failing-id`.
- A schema at `[]` requiring `:user` to carry `:email` still rejects `:n/inc`, because the root changed.
- A parent schema at `[:a]` still rejects an invalid write to `[:a :b]`.
- The existing boot-window behaviour is unchanged: an absent non-nullable slice still rejects.
- Validator calls per commit equal the changed registered slices plus the absent ones.
- Gates: the schemas JVM lane and the core JVM lane (router change), plus CLJS via the PR's CI.

## Notes

- Origin: Opus review (probed); Sol 10 §2 confirms the mechanism by reading.
- Related: rf2-2xzc and rf2-ghxt (closed) are the boot-window face of the same all-paths rule. They were fixed in the examples with `[:maybe …]`, not in the validator. Per rf2-2xzc's measured account, a rejected candidate also skips its `:fx`, so nothing downstream of a refused event fires either. rf2-s8sth (open, schemas prune follow-ups) touches docstrings in the same files but not this behaviour.
- Independent of the schemas memo-growth bead in this batch: they touch different code (`validate.cljc` and the router here, `cache.cljc`/`validator.cljc`/`walker.cljc` there), so they can run in parallel.
- Hot zones: none. `spec/010-Schemas.md` and `router.cljc` are not on the list. The hook's signature changes, so the core router call site and the schemas implementation move in one PR, along with its row in `implementation/core/src/re_frame/late_bind/directory.cljc:293`.
- Supporting detail: `ai/findings/advisarial-review/opus/schemas.md` decision 4 and action 2; `ai/findings/advisarial-review/sol/10-schemas.md` §2.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY 2026-10-10 (PR #11063, branch worker/schemas-review) ==
Verdict: FIXED. The premise held at trunk e9ba1bb2a3. The probe reproduced it: after re-registering [:user] to require :email, each :n/inc was rejected with :failing-id :n/inc.

Fix (minimal direction as the mayor chose it; first-registration extension NOT taken):
- router.cljc run-candidate-validation! takes db-before, which is the handler-scoped :db coeffect (path rule 6 restores it to the pre-event root). The app-db arm passes db-before as the hook's 5th arg, `(validate db-after event-id frame continue? db-before)`. The machine-data arm is unchanged.
- validate.cljc: validate-app-schema! gains a 5-arity. When db-before is supplied, it skips a registered path whose slice is present in both dbs and identical?. A parent path is still checked when a write lands beneath it, [] whenever the db changed, and an absent slice always. Arities 1 to 4 check every entry, as before.
- The late-bind directory row :schemas/validate-app-schema! now names the 5-arg signature. docs/api/re-frame.schemas.md lists the arity.
- Spec 010: §When schemas are checked (row and a new paragraph stating the guarantee) and §Schema migration on hot-reload (one sentence). Guarantee as written: every value a commit writes at a registered path conforms, and a value left in place across a re-registration is named by :rf.schema/violation. A first registration emits nothing, so a non-conforming value already present there is reported when an event next writes it.

Tests (implementation/schemas/test):
- schemas-reg-side-effects-test/a-stale-slice-blocks-only-the-events-that-write-it (the bead's probe; also covers the invalid [:user] write and the [] root schema).
- validate-before-install-test/a-commit-checks-only-the-registered-slices-it-changes-or-lacks (counting validator; also covers parent [:a] vs [:a :b] and an absent non-nullable slice).
- Red at base: exit 1 (6 failures). Green: exit 0. Red again with validate.cljc+router.cljc reverted alone: exit 1 (same 6 failures). Restore verified by blob hash equal to HEAD.
- schemas-test/schema-fires-only-on-the-frame-it-registers-against wrote the same string twice, so its second write left [:n] identical and was correctly skipped. Each dispatch now writes its own value.

Residual, recorded for Mike's open question (not acted on): a user interceptor that rewrites the :db coeffect and leaves it rewritten would make db-before that value rather than the installed db. The flow pass already makes the same assumption.
== RULED 2026-10-16 (dossier ruling) ==
This fix deliberately kept checking absent registered slices on every commit until a ruling was made (`spec/010-Schemas.md:158`, `:829`). That ruling is now made. Mike directed that every decision-dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned, and both agreed on the following rules:
- An absent app-db path is not checked.
- A present value, `nil` included, is checked.
- Whether a key must exist is the job of the parent or root schema, as with Malli's `:map`.
- A first registration checks a value that is already present.

The work is filed as rf2-n68h3, followed by rf2-0fa20 and rf2-bvai9.
close_reason: Merged as PR #11063 at 5550acaba9. The router passes the pre-event app-db (the event's :db coeffect) to validate-app-schema! as a fifth argument, and a registered path whose value is present and identical? before and after is skipped; a parent path is still checked when something beneath it changes, [] whenever the db changed, and an absent value on every commit. The optional first-registration extension was not taken. Spec 010 §When schemas are checked and §Schema migration on hot-reload updated. Red at base e9ba1bb2a3 exit 1 (6 failures), green exit 0, red again exit 1 (same 6). Schemas lane 110/319 -> 113/326 as predicted. For Mike's open never-written-slice question: a first registration over a present, non-conforming value is now reported only when an event next changes that value (Spec 010 says so); and an interceptor that rewrites the :db coeffect makes the validator compare against the rewritten value, the same assumption the flow pass already makes.

description:
GATED OPERATOR ACT. NOT ANALYSIS, NOT WORKER WORK. The decision is RULED; what
remains is a checklist and one irreversible push.

RULED 2026-09-09 (dossier + independent Codex review weighed, both reached the
same answer): OPTION A — one tag, v0.0.1.alpha, publishes ALL FOURTEEN
framework artefacts to io.github.day8/* in a single run. Not a pilot subset,
not a hold. RE-CONFIRMED 2026-09-13 by a second delegated pass (dossier + Codex
review): option A stands, and the push condition is every row of the ORDERED
CHECKLIST green, in order, on the merged release commit — the trigger being
Mike's own decision to make the library installable, not a date. THAT
CHECKLIST, with each command and its expected reading, the point of no return,
the half-set recovery, the corrections to older figures, and the notes for the
rename / release-commit / proof workers, is in the note headed
"== RULING (delegated by Mike, 2026-09-13, dossier + Codex review) ==" — the
NEWEST text on this bead; read it first. THE FULL RUNBOOK IS IN THE NOTES ON
THIS BEAD: pre-flight checklist B1-B9 with the exact command and expected
output for each, the copy-pasteable tag sequence, the irreversibility section,
the 14-artefact roster, and what is out of scope.

THE SHAPE IS NOT OPEN. release.yml has exactly one trigger, a tag glob, and no
workflow_dispatch; its first job hard-fails unless the tag equals "v" plus
VERSION, and VERSION reads 0.0.1.alpha. So v0.0.1.alpha is the only valid
first tag, and the tag STARTS publication automatically — there is no
intervening approval step.

BLOCKER CHAIN, both gates start with Mike:
  rf2-uelji (Clojars group badge, ~10 min, publishes nothing, AVAILABLE NOW —
  it is NOT deferred; the 2026-09-16 date in this bead's older notes is stale)
    -> rf2-fo4ng (rename all 19 coordinates to io.github.day8/*)
      -> rf2-pdbe (the CHANGELOG-only release commit; worker PR, Mike merges;
         filed 2026-09-13)
        -> THIS BEAD (token, secrets, push the tag, then a worker proves
           cold-repo artefact-install).
~~Four~~ Five further recorded dependencies are closed: rf2-2hpxo, rf2-i6kh,
rf2-ar67, rf2-7nk1 (the facade sweep) and rf2-kuky.deferrals (measured
2026-09-13 from the dependencies field). The rf2-d1nr BLOCKING row in the notes
is DISCHARGED — rf2-d1nr and its four children closed 2026-09-09/10, PR #9568
merged.

DO NOT TAG UNTIL EVERY BLOCKING ROW IN THE NOTES CHECKLIST IS GREEN. As of
2026-09-13, measured with positive controls: clojars.org/groups/io.github.day8
returns 404 (control: groups/re-frame returns 200), 0 of 19 coordinates
renamed, repository secrets total_count = 0, zero tags and zero releases on
origin. A tag on the tree as it stands would pass lockstep, burn the whole
test job green, then fail at deploy-core (403 expected by analogy with the
2026-05-13 day8/de-dupe attempt; not a canary worth running).

THREE THINGS THAT MUST NOT BE FORGOTTEN AT THE MOMENT OF TAGGING:
  1. NEVER git push --tags. This checkout carries two local-only safety/*
     tags that origin does not have. Push the one tag by name.
  2. Clojars has NO YANK. The point of no return is deploy-core's clein
     deploy step. deploy-leaf runs fail-fast: false, so a single leaf failure
     can leave a PERMANENT public 11-of-14 half-set. Recovery is
     bump-and-supersede to 0.0.1.alpha-1 only — never re-run the same tag
     (409). The one exception, verified: if all fourteen deploys succeeded and
     only github-release failed, re-run that single terminal job.
  3. TESTING.md:67 makes the release tier "release.yml PLUS the latest green
     expensive run on the release candidate" — B8 in the checklist.

OUT OF SCOPE: the five TOOL jars (xray, story, story-mcp, machines-viz,

namespace this project will use forever, as its first ever release.

SINGLE JOB on the original ref. It is terminal: it needs deploy-core,
deploy-leaf, deploy-ssr-ring and deploy-fresco, and NOTHING needs it; it

failed ANNOUNCEMENT. Also note: a failed deploy command can be AMBIGUOUS about

(vii) Codex additions kept because they help the executors: the seven external Maven pins the framework publishes are all live (POM GET 200 for Clojure 1.12.0, ClojureScript 1.12.145, data.json 2.5.1, Reagent 2.0.1, UIx core 1.4.4, Malli 0.20.1, Cheshire 5.13.0 — availability only, not a transitive-compatibility proof); a green deploy job is NOT a registry-resolution test because the leaf jobs install core (and ssr) into the runner's ~/.m2 first (release.yml:518-526 and the two-rewrite stages), which is why the cold-repo proof exists; preflight-reagent-slim-package.sh:129 hard-codes the old-group POM path and flips in the rename.

3. OPTIONS CONSIDERED, one line each on why not

- A — one tag, all fourteen: CHOSEN. The DAG as built; deploy-core-first is the pilot; one operator act either way.
- B — pilot subset first (e.g. core -> ssr -> fresco): not available from the tag without editing release.yml + the 14-publisher pin + policy 3 + the "fourteen" statements; the pilot's publish is as permanent as the real one; a laptop clein deploy of core alone at 0.0.1.alpha makes the later tag 409 and strands the pilot core forever, and at a throwaway version leaves permanent junk. Choose B only for a real product-scope reason (an artefact Mike does not want public at alpha), and then as an explicit policy change to those places — never a quiet subset tag.
- C1 — hold until Mike wants outsiders to install: LEGITIMATE and technically costless; it IS the trigger clause of this ruling. If Mike chooses it as a standing park rather than a pending trigger, say so on rf2-uelji so its re-park path re-arms; silence is not a re-park. Cost while held: the checkout-based install route, the setup skill's :local/root and :git/sha arms, the pilots and the tools tier all stay parked.
- C2 — hold until the pilots have run: inverts the dependency (rf2-hic-063 forbids a pilot before the artefact exists); waits forever. Rejected.
- C3 — hold until the tools tier can ship in the same sitting: rf2-pv7p is deliberately AFTER the framework proof so a bad framework set cannot strand every tool jar. Rejected.
- D — all four tags in one sitting: five more irreversible publishes before the set is proven installable. Rejected.
- D — a different version string: a VERSION edit plus ~36 tracked files hard-coding 0.0.1.alpha for no gain. Rejected.
- D — workflow_dispatch or a dry-run input on release.yml: a second trigger on the one-trigger workflow the policy test pins; rehearse locally instead. Rejected.
- D — per-artefact readiness audit before the tag: a new gate over lockstep + the test job + POM inspection. Rejected; "ready" keeps its narrow form (checklist satisfied, main green).
- D — an unscoped account token: reaches every group mikethompson can deploy to, legacy day8 included. Rejected.
- D — identity override (net.clojars.mikethompson, already verified; or DNS-verified au.com.day8): rf2-uelji's question, not this bead's, and it must be settled BEFORE rf2-fo4ng dispatches. io.github.day8 taken as given here.

THE POINT OF NO RETURN is release.yml:388, clojure -M:clein deploy in deploy-core. Everything before it — the tag check, lockstep, the whole test job — is a free rehearsal of your own tree.

  All fourteen deployed and only github-release red: re-run THAT ONE JOB on the original ref (terminal, needs nothing after it, touches Clojars not at all). No bump.
  Anything else at or after 388 — THE HALF-SET RECOVERY. NEVER re-run the same tag (deploy-core 409s on the duplicate upload and the run looks stuck). Never ask Clojars for a yank.

THREE THINGS NOT TO FORGET AT TAGGING TIME (as the description says):
  1. Never git push --tags — push the one tag by name.
  2. No yank; the point of no return is 388; a leaf failure can leave a permanent 11-of-14; recovery is bump-and-supersede, never the same tag again; the one exception is a red github-release alone.
  3. TESTING.md:67 — the expensive run must be green on the candidate (row 9).

Afterwards the cold-repo install proof is a WORKER's job (Mike may run it; it is not an operator act): the mayor dispatches it the tick after github-release is green, with the BINDING fixture in the 2026-09-04 RULING note, paragraph "THE CORRECTED PROOF FIXTURE" (explicit :shadow alias; a bare :deps true does not work). MAYOR — TWO PUBLISHED-DOCS GAPS ROUTED HERE, 2026-08-18 23:35 AUSEST. Found by rf2-v04s's worker (PR #8501) while writing the pilot briefs under the docs-only independence protocol. Recorded on this bead because this bead is what closes them; they are NOT separate work and no bead is being filed for them.

G1 — THERE IS NO PUBLISHED COORDINATE, so docs/core/hicasso/00-installation.md routes a reader through a monorepo clone and :local/root. A pilot following the published instructions CORRECTLY ends up with the whole repository on disk.

G2 — THE MIGRATION REPORTER IS STEP 1 OF THE PUBLISHED MIGRATION PROCESS AND CANNOT BE REACHED FROM THE PUBLISHED SITE. It runs from migration/reagent-to-hicasso/codemod inside a checkout, and that tree sits in mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs. So a pilot cannot begin the documented process from published material alone.

G3 is milder and is NOT routed here: the compatibility matrix and full upgrade policy live in the site-excluded release-policy.md, but 00-installation.md now publishes a 4-row summary and the substance of the upgrade promise (PR #8498), so that outcome is only partly blind.

WHY G1 AND G2 BELONG TO THIS BEAD RATHER THAN TO A NEW ONE. Both have the same root cause — no artefact to install — and both are discharged by this bead's own deliverable. Cutting the first tag on io.github.day8/* and proving artefact-install is exactly what lets 00-installation.md stop routing through a clone, which is what puts the migration reporter within reach of a reader who has not cloned anything. Filing them separately would create two beads that can only close when this one does.

WHAT THIS COSTS WHILE IT WAITS, so the hold does not read as free. rf2-v04s could not make the pilots blind by ABSENCE, because the published docs themselves put the repository on the pilot's disk. Its worker therefore built blinding as a READ FENCE enforced by citation — every friction-log entry names where its answer came from, and a published page is the only clean source. That is a good design and it survives G1 closing, but it exists because of G1. When you cut the tag, re-read the pilot briefs: the read fence can relax to a genuine absence, and rf2-hic-069's fresh-reader audit gets stronger for it.

This note is a CLAIM — re-derive both gaps at the tip before acting on them.

RE-TESTED AT SOURCE. rf2-uelji reads DEFERRED with deferred_until 2026-09-16, and its description states the mechanism: Clojars requires a NEW project to live in a VERIFIED group, verification requires a reverse-domain group name, and 'day8' is not reverse-domain and therefore cannot be verified. Existing projects in an old group may publish new versions; a new project may not be created. So no worker clears this — it is a policy question about a coordinate, not work.

WHAT THE HOLD IS COSTING, recorded because a hold with no cost written on it reads as free. This bead is the ONLY thing between Hicasso and a consumable artefact. Measured this morning: 86 of 90 hic-NNN beads closed, 28 source files and ~17,200 lines shipping under implementation/hicasso/src, 446 test files, 29 published guide pages carried in mkdocs nav, and the adapter registered in every roster. The documentary half of the original rf2-hic-061 clause — versioning and release automation, the 14-row compatibility matrix, the upgrade policy including complaint-id stability — is done and closed. What cannot be demonstrated is the one clause that matters to a consumer: that an app can install Hicasso from the artefact rather than from this repository.

title: Pair MCP snapshot: route the :traces slice through project-egress (it is the one slice that skips the off-box projection)
description:
The pair MCP's `snapshot` tool returns five slices: `:app-db`, `:sub-cache`, `:machines`, `:epochs` and `:traces`. Four of them go through the off-box projection door, `re-frame.core/project-egress`, before they leave the runtime. `:traces` does not. It is a possible privacy leak, found by reading the source; it has not been run.

## Evidence (read in source at trunk 89517e8f54)

- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/args.cljs:28` lists the slices `#{:app-db :sub-cache :machines :epochs :traces}`.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/snapshot.cljs:165-193` builds the per-slice walk:
  - `:app-db` goes through `project-egress`;
  - `:sub-cache` goes through `project-egress` per entry;
  - `:epochs` goes through `egress/project-page-src`;
  - `:machines` becomes `:rf/redacted`.
  - There is no `:traces` arm. A search for `traces` in `snapshot.cljs` finds nothing.
- The only gate on `:traces` is the whole-event drop in `tools/sensitive.cljs`, which strips items carrying a sensitivity flag (docstring ~L98). So an UNFLAGGED trace bundle ships with emit-time projection only. It skips the off-box fail-closed rules that the epoch tools apply to event arguments, effect arguments and HTTP bodies.

The decision dossier on the pair MCP's whole-event drop recommends replacing that drop with redacted skeletons. If it lands, the drop goes and `:traces` loses its only gate, so this fix must land first or in the same change.

## Change

Do one of the following:
- route `:traces` items through the same epoch trace projector the `:epochs` slice uses;
- or retire the `:traces` slice from `snapshot`, if `trace-window` / `watch-epochs` already serve it.

Then update the catalogue (`tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/spec/003-Tool-Catalogue.md`) and the tool descriptor text in `descriptors_data.cljs` (~L896, L912, L989, L1011) to match.

No hot-zone files are touched.

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\decisions\mcp-whole-event-drop-for-sensitive-events.md` (Adjacent questions). That file may already be deleted; this bead is self-contained.
acceptance_criteria:
1. First prove the gap is real: a `snapshot` call with `:traces` on an app whose trace carries a distinctive secret in an event argument, an effect argument or an HTTP body, with no sensitivity flag, returns that secret. It must go red at base.
2. After the change, the same call returns no secret. Either the slice is projected exactly as `:epochs` is, or the slice is gone.
3. The catalogue and the descriptor text describe what the slice now does.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY (PR #11362, branch worker/pair-mcp-traces-egress, base dbb2b1a0bd)

Option taken: PROJECT, not retire. The :traces slice stays in snapshot's vocabulary; each event bundle is projected.

Change (tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp only):
- epoch_egress.cljs: new project-trace-bundles-src. Each bundle's :trace-events crosses re-frame.core/project-egress inside a record stamped :kind :rf/epoch-record (bundle's own :frame, no other slot), under the SAME opts as the :epochs slice (egress-opts-edn incl?: off-box-tool, plus include-sensitive? only on the two-key opt-in). That is the only door that reaches the epoch projector's trace-event rules (elide-trace-events-slot: event args, fx-arg carriers, HTTP bodies, resource keys, large sub values, then the bulk walk). The bundle is then rebuilt from the projected events with the ring's own fold (re-frame.trace.projection/absorb over empty-event-bundle, as trace-buffer builds it), so :event/:dispatched/:handler/:fx/:effects/:subs/:renders/:other/:parent-dispatch-id are views of the projected events.
- snapshot.cljs: the slice walk gains an unconditional :traces arm calling it.
- egress_elision_test.cljs: form-level pin snapshot-traces-slice-crosses-the-epoch-projector (gate off; gate off + hostile include-sensitive; gate on + include-sensitive; gate on + elision false).

title: Spec: name :rf/default the conventional single-app frame id (still no runtime privilege)
description:
## Ruling

**`:rf/default` is the conventional, documented frame id for a single-frame app, and every teaching surface converges on it.** Today the repo teaches three ids for the same thing: `:rf/default` (examples, scaffold, getting-started, test fixture, migration, pair MCP), `:app` (the guide) and `:app/main` (the skills and parts of the spec). After this ruling the scaffold, examples, guide, skills and spec boot templates all write `:rf/default` for a single-app frame.

It is a NAMING CONVENTION ONLY:

- `frame-root` keeps its REQUIRED `:id`, written out on the page. A missing `:id` still raises `:rf.error/frame-root-missing-id`.
- The runtime still never creates, infers or falls back to `:rf/default`: it is not created by `init!`, not the React-context default, not a lookup tier. A rootless `dispatch` still raises `:rf.error/no-frame-context`.
- Apps stay free to choose any other id. Descriptive ids stay wherever a passage teaches genuinely independent frames (two roots, per-request SSR frames, stories, embedded widgets).
- Wording constraint: describe it as a shared TEACHING convention, never as an address the REPL or tools secretly expect. Tool-Pair tier 3 resolves any sole app frame whatever its id (`spec/Tool-Pair.md:498`), and the pair guard merely exempts `:rf/default` from reserved-tool classification.
- Matching the app's id and the test fixture's id helps orientation, not test fidelity: the fixture builds `:preset :test` and does not mount the production root, so its `:fx-overrides` / `:interceptors` are not reproduced. Do not claim otherwise.

Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned:

> review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section.  Where the original recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision.  And then remove the file.  Leave behind cases where the two differ materially.

Both the original dossier recommendation and the independent Codex review chose option A (bless the name, keep `:id` required, align the guide and skills) and both deferred B.

**Decisive facts (at trunk 89517e8f54):**

1. **The newcomer path fails silently today.** `docs/core/getting-started.md:97` builds the counter with `(def app-frame :rf/default)`. The next guide page, `docs/core/app-db.md:109`, says "call `(rf/app-db-value :app)`", and `app-db-value` returns `nil` for an unknown frame (`spec/API.md:692`). So the instruction returns `nil` on the app the reader just built. Census: `:rf/default` in 41 example files and the template (`tools/template/resources/day8/re_frame2_template/_reagent/core.cljs:17`); `:app` as a frame id across about 67 files under `docs/` (e.g. `docs/core/introduction.md:51`, `docs/core/how-to/boot-and-mount-an-app.md:46` `(def app-frame :app)`); `:app/main` in the skills and spec (e.g. `skills/re-frame2/references/fundamentals/project-structure.md:106`, which tells readers to pick a "descriptively-named" id and calls `:rf/default` "worth picking only for a tiny app or v1 migration").
2. **The spec still calls the id merely ordinary**, at `spec/002-Frames.md:234-249` and `:900-911`, following EP-0002 resolved open issue 4 (`docs/EP/EP-0002-frame-target-resolution.md:1278-1283`). That issue's premise was that "the reservation buys neither migration nor docs clarity", and it no longer holds. Migration rule M-20 rewrites `:re-frame/default` to `:rf/default` (`migration/from-re-frame-v1/README.md:1022`, row at `:1034`), and the guide calls a single-frame app "Type A — only `:rf/default` in play" (`:696`). The test fixture ensures "the conventional `:rf/default` app frame" (`spec/008-Testing.md:196`, `:216`). The pair guard exempts it as "the canonical app frame" (`tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/reserved_frame_guard.cljs:60-71`).
3. **`frame-root` requires `:id` and fails loud without it** (`spec/002-Frames.md:1696`, `:1746` "There is no `:rf/default` floor"; the shared validator `require-frame-root-id!` is at `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views/frame_boundary.cljs:143-166`). That stays, so this ruling needs no code change.

**Rejected options:**

- **B (an id-less `frame-root` defaults to `:rf/default`): deferred, not taken.** It hides the REPL address from the source. It also gives `frame-root {}` and `make-frame {}` different meanings for "no id": the conventional frame against a private gensym. And it makes silently joining a shared frame the easy path: a second id-less root replaces the first root's `:fx-overrides`/`:interceptors` and never replays its `:initial-events`. Revisit only with evidence that `:rf.error/frame-root-missing-id` is a recurring stumble.
- **C (examples move to app-chosen ids):** the REPL address varies per app, new apps diverge permanently from M-20-migrated apps and from the fixture default, and the guide would still have to pick one id.
- **D (leave as is):** keeps the three-way split and the silent `(rf/app-db-value :app)` failure.
- **Renaming to a non-"default" `:rf/*` id:** about 2,600 occurrences in about 800 files for a wording nuance, and it loses the v1 echo of `:re-frame/default`.
- **Rootless calls resolving to the sole live frame:** stays closed. A callback captured in a destroyed frame would land in its sole successor.

**Supersedes:** the framing of EP-0002 resolved open issue 4 that `:rf/default` is merely an "ordinary" id. Its substance stands: no privilege, no inference, no floor. This ruling does NOT reopen rf2-78wg or rf2-mhpo; their "there is no `:rf/default` floor" corrections stay true and must survive every rewrite.

**Filed as four beads** (label `dossier-ruling`): the spec bead first, then the guide sweep, the examples comment sweep and the skills sweep, which can run in parallel once the spec bead has merged.

## Work (this bead: the spec)

- **`spec/002-Frames.md`**
  - Retitle and rewrite §"`:rf/default` is an ordinary id" (`:234-249`) and §"`:rf/default`" (`:900-911`) as **the conventional app-frame id (no runtime privilege)**. Say three things. By convention a single-frame app names its frame `:rf/default`. The scaffold, examples, guide, test-support fixture and v1 migration (M-20) all use that name. And, unchanged: it is not created by `init!`, not the React-context default, not a lookup tier, and not inferred from a missing `:rf.frame/id`, so absence is `:rf.error/no-frame-context`, never a silent selection of `:rf/default`.
  - The only inbound anchor to the retitled heading is `spec/002-Frames.md:903` (`#rfdefault-is-an-ordinary-id`; `git grep` found no other at trunk 89517e8f54). Update it to the new slug.
  - Line 17: keep "There is **no** process-global `:rf/default`…". Where it fits, add that `:rf/default` is the conventional name an app writes at its own root.
  - `:93`, `:1696` and `:1746` stay as they are: `:id` is required, and there is no floor.
- **`spec/Conventions.md:8` and `:189`**: word the carve-out as "`:rf/default`, the conventional app-frame id an app or test MAY explicitly register (the runtime never synthesises it)".
- **`spec/Tool-Pair.md:505`**: change the carve-out's "ordinary app-frame id" to "conventional app-frame id". Keep tier 3's "regardless of whether it is `:rf/default` or some other id" (`:498`) and the `:507` paragraph rejecting a tier-4 fallback to `:rf/default`.
  - Align the pair guard's docstrings in `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/reserved_frame_guard.cljs`. At `:64`, "the canonical app frame" becomes "the conventional app frame". At `:46-49`, the ns docstring says Conventions.md names `:rf/default` "the universal default frame id"; Conventions.md says no such thing, so quote the new Conventions wording instead. These are comment-only changes; the code stays.
- **`docs/EP/EP-0002-frame-target-resolution.md`** resolved open issue 4 (`:1278-1283`): append a follow-up note dated 2026-10-16. It says the id is now the documented conventional app-frame id with no runtime privilege, and why: M-20, the fixture default and the pair carve-out made the reservation useful after all. Keep the original text; EPs are design records.
- **Spec single-app boot TEMPLATES** (recipes a reader copies to start an app) move from `:app/main` to `:rf/default`:
  - `spec/Pattern-Boot.md:262`;
  - `spec/Construction-Prompts.md:848` (the `frame-root` wiring template) and `:1006-1012` (the SSR client `run`);
  - `spec/011-SSR.md:483-486` (the hydrating client `run`).
- **Deliberately stays:**
  - Spec passages that illustrate a per-call frame argument or a multi-frame situation may keep a descriptive id. Examples: `spec/Tool-Pair.md:218-292`, `spec/015-Data-Classification.md:223-376`, `spec/016-Resources.md:752-760`, `spec/002-Frames.md:1069`, `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:995`, `spec/009-Instrumentation.md:1245`, `spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:536`. Change one only if it is plainly a single-app boot.
  - No code change. The fixture (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/test_support.cljc:855-877`), the template, the pair guard's logic and the examples already conform. There is no new warning, lint, error-message change or constructor change; option B is explicitly not taken.
  - `re-frame.trace.projection` files frameless dispatch traces under `:rf/default` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/projection.cljc:139`). That is a separate question, out of scope here.

## Sequencing

- **Hot zones touched:** `spec/002-Frames.md`, `spec/Conventions.md`, `spec/Tool-Pair.md`. Run this bead alone against any other bead touching those three files.
- **`spec/011-SSR.md` is the one i/crlf file** in the tree. Edit it with the Edit tool or Python bytes, never `sed -i`. Afterwards confirm with Python that total CR == CRLF pairs and bare LF == 0, and that `git ls-files --eol spec/011-SSR.md` still reads `i/crlf`. The other edited files are `w/crlf`; take the same three numbers on each.
- **Depends on:** nothing inside this ruling. **Blocks:** the guide-sweep, examples-comment and skills beads filed beside it.
- **Cross-dossier:** sequence this bead (not parallel) with whatever beads come from `ssr-server-init-reserved-name.md`, which rewrites the same `spec/Conventions.md:8` carve-out sentence and touches `spec/011-SSR.md` and `spec/002-Frames.md`. Do the same for `one-registry-top-level-reg.md`, which touches `spec/002-Frames.md` and `spec/Conventions.md`. Also check the bead from `dispatch-sync-rethrow.md` (the other half of the same corpus question, Q10) if it touches `spec/002-Frames.md`.
- **Gates:**
  - `mkdocs build --strict` plus `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`. The retitled heading changes an anchor slug, which only `check_doc_slugs.py` grades.
  - No gate reads the ids themselves; check those by hand and say so in the PR body.
  - The docstring edits in `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp` are comment-only.

## Evidence

Every path:line above was read in source at trunk 89517e8f54 and re-read unchanged at 3aaacf1cde (`git diff --stat 89517e8f54 3aaacf1cde` is empty over spec, docs, skills, examples, implementation, tools and migration). Nothing here needs a run: the change is spec prose plus two docstrings.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Both `:rf/default` passages in `spec/002-Frames.md` (formerly `:234-249` and `:900-911`) say that `:rf/default` is the conventional app-frame id for a single-frame app. They still say that it is not created by `init!`, not inferred from a missing frame stamp and not a lookup tier, and that absence raises `:rf.error/no-frame-context`. `:93`, `:1696` (`:id` required) and `:1746` (no `:rf/default` floor) are unchanged.
2. `spec/Conventions.md:8` and `:189` describe the carve-out as the conventional app-frame id, which the runtime never synthesises.
3. `spec/Tool-Pair.md:505` says "conventional app-frame id". Tier 3 still resolves any sole app frame whatever its id, and the tier-4 no-fallback paragraph is intact. The pair guard docstrings in `reserved_frame_guard.cljs` (`:46-49` and `:64`) say "conventional" and no longer quote a Conventions phrase that does not exist.
4. EP-0002 resolved open issue 4 keeps its original text and carries an appended follow-up note dated 2026-10-16.
5. The single-app boot templates use `:rf/default`: `spec/Pattern-Boot.md:262`, `spec/Construction-Prompts.md:848` and `:1006-1012`, and `spec/011-SSR.md:483-486`.
6. `git grep -n 'rfdefault-is-an-ordinary-id'` returns nothing. `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` and `mkdocs build --strict` both exit 0, with the exit codes quoted in the PR body.
7. The diff touches no code: the only file outside `spec/` and `docs/EP/` is `reserved_frame_guard.cljs`, and only its docstrings change. A Python count on each edited file shows CR == CRLF and zero bare LF, and `spec/011-SSR.md` still reads `i/crlf`.
